2.3 X-Ray Computed Tomography

    In X-ray computed tomography (CT), X-ray radiographs from hundreds of different angles are taken of
a sample. Contrast comes from differences between the X-ray attenuation characteristics for each kind of
material. Mathematical algorithms use this information to reconstruct the interior of the sample. Output is
in the form of hundreds or thousands of cross-sectional images, which can be stacked together to form a
3-D image of the sample. A special procedure for acquiring and analyzing star-shaped particles via a
combination of X-ray CT and spherical harmonic series was used [15,16]. “Star-shaped” is a weaker
condition than convexity and essentially means that there is a point in the interior of the particles from
which a line segment can be drawn to the exterior by only crossing the particle surface once [15,16]. The
metallic powders were embedded in 3 mm diameter epoxy cylinders, and images were taken at a pixel size
of about 2 µm. The images were 2000 × 2000 pixels square, or about 4 mm × 4 mm. Once the slices were
assembled into a 3-D structure, a gray scale threshold was applied to make the particles white and the
background black. Special software extracted the particles and analyzed their shape using spherical
harmonic series, which gave a mathematical representation for each star-shaped particle. The particles that
were judged by the software to not be star-shaped were usually two or more particles stuck together, either
in reality or because of the thresholding.
  A goal of this current work is to show how different samples taken from nominally identical powder
may differ from each other in their shape and size distribution. The size distribution was also measured by
laser diffraction, but the CT gives an independent estimate and uses different size parameters to measure
the PSD. However, it uses fewer particles, so the particle size distribution curves are generally not as
smooth. The SEM gives detailed images of the particles, and can give some degree of perspective also, so
that the images can be quasi-3D. But the X-ray CT gives direct, 3-D shape information about the particles.
This particle shape is the focus of this section.
   To make samples for both the 17-4SS and CoCr powders, a dilute suspension of the particles was
created in a marine epoxy [16]. The volume fraction of powder in the suspension varied, but was usually
only a few percent by volume. After vigorous stirring, to make sure that the particles were suspended, a
laboratory vacuum line was used to draw up the suspension into a plastic straw of about 2 mm inner
diameter and length about 12 cm. The straw was capped at both ends with putty, put into a 4 cm diameter
cylinder of polymer insulating rigid foam, and then rotated continuously while curing to minimize powder
settling effects in the epoxy. After cure, the ends were cut off and the sample was divided into a larger and
a smaller piece. Usually the larger piece by itself gave enough particles for analysis. The larger sample
piece was put upright into an aluminum sample holder and placed into a commercial X-ray CT machine.
All samples were scanned at about 2 µm per voxel. A typical sample gave 6000 slices, where each slice

Appendix 4: Powder Sampling12

Reliable powder sampling  is obligatory for  all particle characterisation procedures. The
sample collected from the bulk must be representative of the entire physical and chemical
characteristics of the system in order for derived data to contain any meaning. According to
the ‘Golden Rule of Sampling’:

    A powder should be sampled when in motion
     The whole sample stream should be taken over many short time increments, rather
       than part of the stream being taken for the whole of the time.

During bulk sampling, issues arise due to powder segregation. Variation exists in different
regions of a heap or container and also between sample containers. If static sampling must be
employed, samples should be taken from many random positions in different bags or
containers, and later combined to form as representative a sample as possible. In the case of
heap sampling, if possible the heap should be mixed prior to sampling.

There are a variety of different sub-sampling methods which can be used to turn a bulk
sample into a more manageable laboratory sample.

Cone and quartering

The powder is formed into a cone shaped heap on a flat surface, before being flattened with a
spatula and divided into four identical volumes. One portion is taken and the entire procedure
is repeated until only 1/16th of the original volume remains. This method is heavily operator
dependant and  is only suitable for powders with poor flow behaviour and thus  little
segregation. Large particles will tend to roll to the outside edges of the heap as it is made,
while fine material will adhere to the working surface, thus narrowing the final overall size
distribution.

Scoop Sampling

The operator manually scoops a small portion of powder from the bulk sample. Only
appropriate for homogenous materials with poor flow characteristics.

Table Sampling

The sample moves down an inclined plane, prisms divert and control the flow so that aliquots
of sample fall through holes in the table. The powder that is collected at the end of the table is
the required sub-sample (Figure A3.1).  Initial feed should be representative and mixed
thoroughly, to eliminate the main source of variation.

Chute

The sample is introduced into a V shaped trough, feeding through a number of chutes, and
collected in two trays on either side of the trough. The procedure is repeated with the powder
in one tray, until the desired amount is obtained. The trough must be loaded without causing
sample segregation.

Spin Riffling

A spinning riffler (see Figure A3.2) divides the sample into a series of glass containers.
Powder is transported from the hopper, via a vibratory chute, into a series of containers
rotating at a constant speed. The sample flows into the receivers at a constant rate causing
them to be filled uniformly. The drawback to this method is that the sample volume is
relatively small, handling powders in grams and milligrams.

{"answer": "# Repeatability and reproducibility of metal-powder characterization

**The available evidence does not establish a single ASTM/ISO precision value for each requested measurement.** In particular, I could not verify an ASTM B214/ISO 4497 precision-and-bias table giving the standard deviation of *mass retained in each sieve cut*, or an ASTM B822/ISO 13320 interlaboratory table giving D10, D50, and D90 coefficients of variation for AM metal powder. The numerical studies below are useful comparators, but a variation between containers measured in one laboratory is **not** between-laboratory reproducibility, and variation between particles is **not** repeatability of a reported powder mean. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017)

## 1. Sieve analysis: ASTM B214 / ISO 4497

For each cut, the appropriate result is retained mass divided by the initial test-portion mass; its repeatability standard deviation must be estimated from **independently sampled and sieved test portions**. None of the accessible evidence provides a defensible universal standard deviation, in percentage points of retained mass, for a particular cut under either standard. Cut-dependent effects matter: particles near an aperture, sieve loading, lodged particles, and the condition of the mesh can change retention. A powder-characterization handbook identifies ISO 4497 and ASTM B214 as corresponding metal-powder sieving methods and describes weighing the residue on each sieve, but does not supply an interlaboratory precision table. (pqac-00000051)

One NIST study did sieve IN625 powder from different participant containers following **ASTM B214** and reported derived size percentiles: D10 = **18.46 ± 3.77 µm**, D50 = **34.32 ± 1.74 µm**, and D90 = **49.95 ± 1.08 µm**. These are *not* standard deviations of retained mass per sieve cut. Samples from participant containers were analyzed by NIST; this was not an interlaboratory comparison of sieve measurements, despite the interlaboratory AM-build study in which the powder was used. The implied percentile CVs are approximately **20.4%, 5.1%, and 2.2%**, respectively, and must not be presented as ASTM B214 precision limits. (pqac-00000008)

## 2. Laser diffraction: ISO 13320 / ASTM B822

In a NIST metal-powder study using wet laser diffraction, four **17-4 stainless-steel containers** from one heat lot gave D10 **24.4 ± 0.6 µm**, D50 **36.5 ± 0.2 µm**, and D90 **54.5 ± 0.8 µm**; the corresponding between-container CVs calculated from the reported means and one-standard-deviation spreads are **2.5%, 0.55%, and 1.5%**. Fifteen **CoCr containers** gave **8.9 ± 0.4**, **23.0 ± 0.96**, and **44.7 ± 1.5 µm**, or CVs of approximately **4.5%, 4.2%, and 3.4%**. These spreads combine container, subsampling, and analytical effects under one laboratory’s procedure; neither set is a separately estimated within-laboratory repeatability SD or between-laboratory reproducibility SD. NIST describes its dispersion medium as isopropanol and its measurement procedure as 25 measurements after sonication followed by three sets of six measurements checked for consistency. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000050)

An actual **between-laboratory** round robin in an NPL good-practice guide used **silica, not metal powder**. For its powder extending to approximately 100 µm, D10/D50/D90 between-laboratory CVs were **30.5%/14.0%/7.4%** with a less prescribed procedure and **9.9%/5.0%/4.6%** after a more closely specified procedure. For finer silica extending to approximately 10 µm, the corresponding CVs were **43.7%/20.4%/8.8%** and **35.2%/9.6%/9.5%**. These results demonstrate the potentially large contribution of laboratory-specific sampling and dispersion; they are **not** ISO 13320 or ASTM B822 precision-and-bias limits for metal powders. (pqac-00000017)

## 3. SEM and dynamic image analysis: circularity or sphericity

**There is no source-supported fixed number of particles that guarantees a stable shape mean.** For a *number-weighted* mean of independently sampled particle circularities, a defensible count is determined from the observed between-particle standard deviation, \(s_C\): its sampling standard error is approximately \(s_C/\sqrt n\), and an approximate 95% sampling half-width is \(1.96s_C/\sqrt n\). For illustration—not a measured AM-powder precision claim—if \(s_C=0.10\), **100, 400, and 1,600** representative particles give approximate half-widths of **0.020, 0.010, and 0.005** circularity units, respectively. Independently prepared aliquots and repeated segmentation are still required to assess *measurement* repeatability; counting more particles cannot remove sampling bias or systematic image-analysis error. The result also depends on whether the reported mean is number- or volume-weighted. Mitterlehner and colleagues explicitly use a **volume-weighted** image-analysis sphericity and show that their silhouette-based sphericity definition differs from another commonly termed circularity: in their notation, SPHT = \(4\pi A/P^2=C^2\). (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029)

The stakes of the measurand are illustrated by a NIST SEM study of 17-4 steel powder: it estimated that **59,866 particles** were needed for a **95% probability of no more than 3% relative error in a mass-median *size***, and analyzed **more than 69,000**. That is a distribution-percentile, volume/mass-weighted sizing calculation—**not** a minimum count established for mean circularity. For three repeated dynamic-image-analysis measurements, its average standard uncertainty of *volume fraction per size bin* was **0.02 percentage points wet** and **0.06 percentage points dry**; again, neither number is uncertainty of sphericity. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027)

A metal-powder methods comparison provides a useful warning about **between-method differences**, rather than repeatability: volume-based sphericity for one nearly spherical powder was **0.969 by dynamic imaging**, **0.825 by optical microscopy of polished sections**, and **0.898 by micro-CT**. The authors attribute part of the micro-CT discrepancy to its 1-µm voxel resolution. Consequently, a universal claim of, for example, ±0.01 sphericity across SEM, dynamic imaging, and other geometries would not be justified by these data; no validated typical between-laboratory SD for an AM-powder shape mean was located. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055)

## 4. SEM–EDS composition: Si and Mg in Al-alloy powder

For **polished, homogeneous specimens measured with standards and matrix corrections**, NIST authors describe achievable relative accuracy of approximately **±5% for major constituents** (>10 wt%), **±10% for minor constituents** (1–10 wt%), and **±25% for trace-level constituents** (0.1–1 wt%). These are accuracy guidance, **not repeatability SDs or validated limits for an unpolished AlSi10Mg particle**. Silicon near 10 wt% lies on the major/minor boundary; magnesium below 1 wt% lies in the authors’ trace category. Surface curvature and local topography of loose particles can cause substantially greater error; normalizing a standardless analysis to 100% can conceal it. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040)

As an illustration of *best-controlled repeatability*, not of Al-alloy-powder performance, NIST measured a homogeneous reference **glass** in nine replicate standards-based EDS analyses. Si was **25.38 wt% certified versus 25.65 wt% measured** (**+1.1% relative deviation; 0.09% relative replicate SD**), and Mg was **8.85 versus 8.81 wt%** (**−0.4% relative deviation; 0.13% relative replicate SD**). These high Mg and Si concentrations and polished-glass geometry cannot establish precision for approximately 0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in loose AlSi10Mg powder. No Al-alloy-powder-specific interlaboratory SEM–EDS Si/Mg repeatability or reproducibility estimates were verified. Bulk certification of such low Mg contents should therefore be checked with a validated bulk-composition method rather than inferred from particle-surface EDS alone. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040)

## 5. Powder sampling and its share of total variance

A published powder-sampling comparison reproduced in the NPL guide gives **relative SDs/CVs** of **6.81% for coning and quartering, 5.14% for scoop sampling, 2.09% for table splitting, 1.01% for chute splitting, and 0.125% for a spinning riffler**. These characterize that comparison’s sampled property and powder, **not** a universal CV of every sieve cut or D-value and **not** an ASTM B215 precision-and-bias statement. The guide identifies B215 as a practice for sampling metal powders and recommends taking increments across a moving powder stream; it also notes that segregation adds error beyond fundamental random sampling. A separate experiment with segregating glass-particle mixtures found that a rotary divider could introduce composition-dependent bias, underscoring that owning a rotary device does not itself validate unbiased splitting. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053)

For **independent, approximately unbiased** sources expressed in the *same measurand and units*, a practical variance budget is \(s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\approx s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}}+s^2_{\mathrm{preparation}}+s^2_{\mathrm{instrument}}\). The sampling contribution is \((s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}})/s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\), not the sum of their CVs. The published **0.125%** spinning-riffler CV cannot be inserted directly into an AM-powder D90 or sieve-cut budget: first measure the variation among **independently split test portions**, then compare it with repeated analyses of one portion. As a conditional arithmetic example, if a given measurand has a measured sampling CV of **1%** and analytical CV of **2%**, independent sources imply total CV **2.24%** and sampling accounts for **20% of variance**. Segregation or systematic bias must be assessed separately, not hidden inside this quadrature calculation. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034)

**Bottom line:** the defensible numerical evidence is strongest for NIST’s *single-laboratory, between-container* metal-powder D-value spreads, the *non-metal* laser-diffraction interlaboratory comparison, calibrated-versus-rough-specimen EDS performance, and a *material-specific* splitter comparison. Requested ASTM/ISO **sieve-cut mass-fraction SDs**, metal-powder LD **between-lab CVs**, shape-mean **repeatability SDs**, and AlSi10Mg-specific **Si/Mg EDS repeatability** remain unquantified by the verified sources; assigning them universal numerical tolerances would conflate different measurands and experimental designs. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000054)"}

# Repeatability and reproducibility of metal-powder characterization

**The available evidence does not establish a single ASTM/ISO precision value for each requested measurement.** In particular, I could not verify an ASTM B214/ISO 4497 precision-and-bias table giving the standard deviation of *mass retained in each sieve cut*, or an ASTM B822/ISO 13320 interlaboratory table giving D10, D50, and D90 coefficients of variation for AM metal powder. The numerical studies below are useful comparators, but a variation between containers measured in one laboratory is **not** between-laboratory reproducibility, and variation between particles is **not** repeatability of a reported powder mean. (brown2016interlaboratorystudyfor pages 2-3, slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 8-12, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 40-44)

## 1. Sieve analysis: ASTM B214 / ISO 4497

For each cut, the appropriate result is retained mass divided by the initial test-portion mass; its repeatability standard deviation must be estimated from **independently sampled and sieved test portions**. None of the accessible evidence provides a defensible universal standard deviation, in percentage points of retained mass, for a particular cut under either standard. Cut-dependent effects matter: particles near an aperture, sieve loading, lodged particles, and the condition of the mesh can change retention. A powder-characterization handbook identifies ISO 4497 and ASTM B214 as corresponding metal-powder sieving methods and describes weighing the residue on each sieve, but does not supply an interlaboratory precision table. (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4)

One NIST study did sieve IN625 powder from different participant containers following **ASTM B214** and reported derived size percentiles: D10 = **18.46 ± 3.77 µm**, D50 = **34.32 ± 1.74 µm**, and D90 = **49.95 ± 1.08 µm**. These are *not* standard deviations of retained mass per sieve cut. Samples from participant containers were analyzed by NIST; this was not an interlaboratory comparison of sieve measurements, despite the interlaboratory AM-build study in which the powder was used. The implied percentile CVs are approximately **20.4%, 5.1%, and 2.2%**, respectively, and must not be presented as ASTM B214 precision limits. (brown2016interlaboratorystudyfor pages 2-3)

## 2. Laser diffraction: ISO 13320 / ASTM B822

In a NIST metal-powder study using wet laser diffraction, four **17-4 stainless-steel containers** from one heat lot gave D10 **24.4 ± 0.6 µm**, D50 **36.5 ± 0.2 µm**, and D90 **54.5 ± 0.8 µm**; the corresponding between-container CVs calculated from the reported means and one-standard-deviation spreads are **2.5%, 0.55%, and 1.5%**. Fifteen **CoCr containers** gave **8.9 ± 0.4**, **23.0 ± 0.96**, and **44.7 ± 1.5 µm**, or CVs of approximately **4.5%, 4.2%, and 3.4%**. These spreads combine container, subsampling, and analytical effects under one laboratory’s procedure; neither set is a separately estimated within-laboratory repeatability SD or between-laboratory reproducibility SD. NIST describes its dispersion medium as isopropanol and its measurement procedure as 25 measurements after sonication followed by three sets of six measurements checked for consistency. (slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 8-12, slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 3-4)

An actual **between-laboratory** round robin in an NPL good-practice guide used **silica, not metal powder**. For its powder extending to approximately 100 µm, D10/D50/D90 between-laboratory CVs were **30.5%/14.0%/7.4%** with a less prescribed procedure and **9.9%/5.0%/4.6%** after a more closely specified procedure. For finer silica extending to approximately 10 µm, the corresponding CVs were **43.7%/20.4%/8.8%** and **35.2%/9.6%/9.5%**. These results demonstrate the potentially large contribution of laboratory-specific sampling and dispersion; they are **not** ISO 13320 or ASTM B822 precision-and-bias limits for metal powders. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 40-44)

## 3. SEM and dynamic image analysis: circularity or sphericity

**There is no source-supported fixed number of particles that guarantees a stable shape mean.** For a *number-weighted* mean of independently sampled particle circularities, a defensible count is determined from the observed between-particle standard deviation, \(s_C\): its sampling standard error is approximately \(s_C/\sqrt n\), and an approximate 95% sampling half-width is \(1.96s_C/\sqrt n\). For illustration—not a measured AM-powder precision claim—if \(s_C=0.10\), **100, 400, and 1,600** representative particles give approximate half-widths of **0.020, 0.010, and 0.005** circularity units, respectively. Independently prepared aliquots and repeated segmentation are still required to assess *measurement* repeatability; counting more particles cannot remove sampling bias or systematic image-analysis error. The result also depends on whether the reported mean is number- or volume-weighted. Mitterlehner and colleagues explicitly use a **volume-weighted** image-analysis sphericity and show that their silhouette-based sphericity definition differs from another commonly termed circularity: in their notation, SPHT = \(4\pi A/P^2=C^2\). (mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 3-4, mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 4-5)

The stakes of the measurand are illustrated by a NIST SEM study of 17-4 steel powder: it estimated that **59,866 particles** were needed for a **95% probability of no more than 3% relative error in a mass-median *size***, and analyzed **more than 69,000**. That is a distribution-percentile, volume/mass-weighted sizing calculation—**not** a minimum count established for mean circularity. For three repeated dynamic-image-analysis measurements, its average standard uncertainty of *volume fraction per size bin* was **0.02 percentage points wet** and **0.06 percentage points dry**; again, neither number is uncertainty of sphericity. (whiting2019uncertaintyofparticle pages 2-3, whiting2019uncertaintyofparticle pages 3-4)

A metal-powder methods comparison provides a useful warning about **between-method differences**, rather than repeatability: volume-based sphericity for one nearly spherical powder was **0.969 by dynamic imaging**, **0.825 by optical microscopy of polished sections**, and **0.898 by micro-CT**. The authors attribute part of the micro-CT discrepancy to its 1-µm voxel resolution. Consequently, a universal claim of, for example, ±0.01 sphericity across SEM, dynamic imaging, and other geometries would not be justified by these data; no validated typical between-laboratory SD for an AM-powder shape mean was located. (mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 10-11, mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof media d1ad888f)

## 4. SEM–EDS composition: Si and Mg in Al-alloy powder

For **polished, homogeneous specimens measured with standards and matrix corrections**, NIST authors describe achievable relative accuracy of approximately **±5% for major constituents** (>10 wt%), **±10% for minor constituents** (1–10 wt%), and **±25% for trace-level constituents** (0.1–1 wt%). These are accuracy guidance, **not repeatability SDs or validated limits for an unpolished AlSi10Mg particle**. Silicon near 10 wt% lies on the major/minor boundary; magnesium below 1 wt% lies in the authors’ trace category. Surface curvature and local topography of loose particles can cause substantially greater error; normalizing a standardless analysis to 100% can conceal it. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25)

As an illustration of *best-controlled repeatability*, not of Al-alloy-powder performance, NIST measured a homogeneous reference **glass** in nine replicate standards-based EDS analyses. Si was **25.38 wt% certified versus 25.65 wt% measured** (**+1.1% relative deviation; 0.09% relative replicate SD**), and Mg was **8.85 versus 8.81 wt%** (**−0.4% relative deviation; 0.13% relative replicate SD**). These high Mg and Si concentrations and polished-glass geometry cannot establish precision for approximately 0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in loose AlSi10Mg powder. No Al-alloy-powder-specific interlaboratory SEM–EDS Si/Mg repeatability or reproducibility estimates were verified. Bulk certification of such low Mg contents should therefore be checked with a validated bulk-composition method rather than inferred from particle-surface EDS alone. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 5-6, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25)

## 5. Powder sampling and its share of total variance

A published powder-sampling comparison reproduced in the NPL guide gives **relative SDs/CVs** of **6.81% for coning and quartering, 5.14% for scoop sampling, 2.09% for table splitting, 1.01% for chute splitting, and 0.125% for a spinning riffler**. These characterize that comparison’s sampled property and powder, **not** a universal CV of every sieve cut or D-value and **not** an ASTM B215 precision-and-bias statement. The guide identifies B215 as a practice for sampling metal powders and recommends taking increments across a moving powder stream; it also notes that segregation adds error beyond fundamental random sampling. A separate experiment with segregating glass-particle mixtures found that a rotary divider could introduce composition-dependent bias, underscoring that owning a rotary device does not itself validate unbiased splitting. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 22-26, hawkins1988demonstratingthesampling pages 2-3, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 59-64, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 64-70)

For **independent, approximately unbiased** sources expressed in the *same measurand and units*, a practical variance budget is \(s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\approx s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}}+s^2_{\mathrm{preparation}}+s^2_{\mathrm{instrument}}\). The sampling contribution is \((s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}})/s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\), not the sum of their CVs. The published **0.125%** spinning-riffler CV cannot be inserted directly into an AM-powder D90 or sieve-cut budget: first measure the variation among **independently split test portions**, then compare it with repeated analyses of one portion. As a conditional arithmetic example, if a given measurand has a measured sampling CV of **1%** and analytical CV of **2%**, independent sources imply total CV **2.24%** and sampling accounts for **20% of variance**. Segregation or systematic bias must be assessed separately, not hidden inside this quadrature calculation. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 22-26, hawkins1988demonstratingthesampling pages 3-4)

**Bottom line:** the defensible numerical evidence is strongest for NIST’s *single-laboratory, between-container* metal-powder D-value spreads, the *non-metal* laser-diffraction interlaboratory comparison, calibrated-versus-rough-specimen EDS performance, and a *material-specific* splitter comparison. Requested ASTM/ISO **sieve-cut mass-fraction SDs**, metal-powder LD **between-lab CVs**, shape-mean **repeatability SDs**, and AlSi10Mg-specific **Si/Mg EDS repeatability** remain unquantified by the verified sources; assigning them universal numerical tolerances would conflate different measurands and experimental designs. contexts.context: The excerpt provides only limited quantitative information relevant to the requested uncertainty and sampling details. For dynamic image analysis (DIA) particle-size percentiles, the authors propagated uncertainty using a Monte Carlo simulation with 500,000 iterations. The combined standard uncertainty included four components: calibrated SEM uncertainty (ucal), DIA measurement uncertainty (umeas), systematic SEM–DIA bias (ubias), and sample-to-sample uncertainty (usample). The study treated usample as negligible because the same powder batch was used and samples were collected by riffling. The excerpt also reports that DIA results from dry and wet dispersion were similar; deviation from calibrated SEM data was smallest at or below D10, increased through D50, and reached a maximum near 45 μm (the excerpt displays “45 mm,” likely a formatting or transcription issue) below D90. It does not report the requested original numerical data for particle sphericity/circularity convergence, sample counts, standard deviations of repeated SEM or imaging runs, calibrated versus standardless SEM-EDS Si/Mg relative errors in aluminum alloys, ASTM B215 riffle or spinning-riffler coefficients of variation, or their contributions to total variance.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports Mg and Si results for NIST SRM 470 glass compositions K411 and K412, but it does not include the requested NIST SRM glass K2496 or mineral-standard data. For K411, with oxygen obtained by assumed stoichiometry, certified Mg is 0.0885 mass fraction and measured Mg is 0.0881, giving an RDEV of −0.4% and a relative SD of 0.13% over nine replicates. Certified Si is 0.2538 and measured Si is 0.2565, with RDEV +1.1% and relative SD 0.09%. With oxygen directly analyzed using MgO, K411 Mg is measured as 0.0870 (RDEV −1.6%, relative SD 0.17%), while Si is 0.2525 (RDEV −0.12%, relative SD 0.07%). For K412 under assumed-stoichiometry oxygen, Mg is 0.1166 certified versus 0.1160 measured (−0.48%, 0.23% relative SD), and Si is 0.2120 versus 0.2136 (+0.75%, 0.09%). The alternate K412 table gives Mg 0.1153 against 0.1161 (−1.1%, 0.14%) and Si 0.2120 against 0.2120 (0%, 0.49%). These Mg concentrations are 8.85–11.66 wt%, not minor Mg below 1 wt%. Thus, this excerpt mainly supports approximately ±1–2% accuracy and sub-1% replicate precision for these glass measurements, rather than the requested sub-1-wt% Mg performance.

contexts.context: Mitterlehner et al. report method-dependent particle-shape results for metal additive-manufacturing powders, but the excerpt does not provide stability as a function of particle count, replicate-specimen standard deviations, or a direct circularity metric. The reported parameter is volume-based sphericity (SPHT3), alongside aspect ratio. For powders A, B, and C, lCT sphericities are 0.898, 0.833, and 0.800; DIA values are approximately 0.969/0.968, 0.882/0.877, and 0.893/0.895 (using minimum chord length/area-equivalent diameter); and OMA values are approximately 0.825/0.823, 0.608/0.610, and 0.609/0.613. Results are essentially unchanged between the two DIA and OMA size definitions. OMA gives substantially lower sphericity than DIA, while lCT lies between them. The authors attribute lCT’s unexpectedly low value for highly spherical powder A partly to 1-µm cubic voxels and limited resolution. lCT analyzes particles as three-dimensional objects, whereas OMA analyzes a polished cross-sectional silhouette, creating a 2D-versus-3D bias and shifting apparent size distributions smaller. The excerpt discusses particle counts and fixed versus weighed sample quantities, but does not distinguish number-weighted from volume-weighted mean sphericity; SPHT3 is explicitly volume-based, not necessarily a volume-weighted population mean.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides methodological context for Whiting et al.’s dynamic image analysis (DIA) uncertainty study, but it does not include the referenced NIST Table 1 or the requested numerical distinctions between systematic error and expanded (k=2) uncertainty. The study’s measurand is equivalent circular area diameter (ECAD), and particle-size distributions are reported through volume-based D10, D50, and D90 percentiles. The authors identify numerous possible uncertainty sources, including optical distortion, focus and defocus, motion blur, particle velocity, contamination, overlapping or incompletely imaged particles, orientation, pixel calibration, background correction, edge determination, and size determination across orientations. Their SEM-based calibration strategy was designed to support uncertainty estimation for metal-powder particle-size and PSD measurements. The excerpt discusses segmentation uncertainty and indicates that detector selection and image-processing settings were used to reduce it, ultimately treating image-processing uncertainty as negligible relative to the uncertainties shown in their results. It does not state whether the Table 1 uncertainty applies to sphericity, particle size alone, or both, and it gives no wet-versus-dry within-run bin percentage points.

contexts.context: Table 1 distinguishes systematic error from expanded uncertainty (2uDIA, with coverage factor k = 2) for particle-size percentiles, not from sphericity or roundness uncertainty. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general NIST guidance for particle-size-distribution measurements, including wet and dry sample preparation, replicate measurements, reporting of d10, d50, and d90, and comparison with certified values using expanded uncertainties. It distinguishes neither systematic error from expanded k=2 uncertainty nor uncertainty components associated with wet versus dry measurements. It also contains no data for Whiting 2019, 17-4 stainless steel, sphericity uncertainty, or within-run bin percentage-point differences. The document states that SRM 114 is a reference material rather than a means for direct instrument calibration, and that agreement is assessed by comparing absolute differences in cumulative volume fraction with appropriate expanded uncertainties. For repeatability, it requires at least three PSD sets for the wet method using the same test portion and three different test portions for the dry method. Thus, this excerpt may help interpret general PSD terminology and replicate practices, but it cannot establish the precise distinctions or numerical values requested from DIA Table 1.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not contain NIST Whiting (2019) DIA Table 1, the 17-4 stainless-steel wet/dry results, or numerical D10, D50, and D90 values. It therefore cannot establish the requested systematic-error versus expanded-k=2 distinction or calculate wet/dry within-run differences in percentage points. It does provide the relevant interpretive framework: expanded uncertainty is derived from standard uncertainty using a coverage factor of 2, with an additional square-root-of-2 factor when evaluating the difference between two independent measurements. Such an uncertainty interval describes expected measurement variation; it is not itself a systematic error. Differences exceeding the tabulated uncertainty may indicate additional sources of variation that should be investigated. The document also emphasizes that particle-size distributions depend strongly on measurement methodology and that laser diffraction assumes spherical particles and known refractive indices. Consequently, a reported uncertainty attached to D10/D50/D90 would ordinarily concern the measured particle-size distribution, while uncertainty arising from nonsphericity is a method/model assumption or potential systematic contribution unless explicitly quantified in the cited table. The excerpt gives no evidence that the requested uncertainty is specifically a sphericity uncertainty, nor does it provide wet/dry within-run percentage-point values.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What is the measurement repeatability (within-lab) and reproducibility (between-lab) of metal powder characterization used for additive manufacturing: (1) sieve analysis per ASTM B214 / ISO 4497 (standard deviation of mass fraction per sieve cut); (2) laser diffraction per ISO 13320 / ASTM B822 (coefficient of variation of D10, D50, D90); (3) SEM or dynamic image analysis of sphericity or circularity (how many particles must be measured for a stable mean, and the typical uncertainty); (4) SEM-EDS quantitative composition of aluminum alloy powders, e.g. Si and Mg in Al alloys (typical relative error and repeatability); (5) powder sampling error (riffling, spinning riffler per ASTM B215) and its contribution to the total variance. Give numeric values with citations, especially ASTM/ISO precision-and-bias statements and interlaboratory studies.

# Repeatability and reproducibility of metal-powder characterization

**The available evidence does not establish a single ASTM/ISO precision value for each requested measurement.** In particular, I could not verify an ASTM B214/ISO 4497 precision-and-bias table giving the standard deviation of *mass retained in each sieve cut*, or an ASTM B822/ISO 13320 interlaboratory table giving D10, D50, and D90 coefficients of variation for AM metal powder. The numerical studies below are useful comparators, but a variation between containers measured in one laboratory is **not** between-laboratory reproducibility, and variation between particles is **not** repeatability of a reported powder mean. (brown2016interlaboratorystudyfor pages 2-3, slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 8-12, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 40-44)

## 1. Sieve analysis: ASTM B214 / ISO 4497

For each cut, the appropriate result is retained mass divided by the initial test-portion mass; its repeatability standard deviation must be estimated from **independently sampled and sieved test portions**. None of the accessible evidence provides a defensible universal standard deviation, in percentage points of retained mass, for a particular cut under either standard. Cut-dependent effects matter: particles near an aperture, sieve loading, lodged particles, and the condition of the mesh can change retention. A powder-characterization handbook identifies ISO 4497 and ASTM B214 as corresponding metal-powder sieving methods and describes weighing the residue on each sieve, but does not supply an interlaboratory precision table. (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4)

One NIST study did sieve IN625 powder from different participant containers following **ASTM B214** and reported derived size percentiles: D10 = **18.46 ± 3.77 µm**, D50 = **34.32 ± 1.74 µm**, and D90 = **49.95 ± 1.08 µm**. These are *not* standard deviations of retained mass per sieve cut. Samples from participant containers were analyzed by NIST; this was not an interlaboratory comparison of sieve measurements, despite the interlaboratory AM-build study in which the powder was used. The implied percentile CVs are approximately **20.4%, 5.1%, and 2.2%**, respectively, and must not be presented as ASTM B214 precision limits. (brown2016interlaboratorystudyfor pages 2-3)

## 2. Laser diffraction: ISO 13320 / ASTM B822

In a NIST metal-powder study using wet laser diffraction, four **17-4 stainless-steel containers** from one heat lot gave D10 **24.4 ± 0.6 µm**, D50 **36.5 ± 0.2 µm**, and D90 **54.5 ± 0.8 µm**; the corresponding between-container CVs calculated from the reported means and one-standard-deviation spreads are **2.5%, 0.55%, and 1.5%**. Fifteen **CoCr containers** gave **8.9 ± 0.4**, **23.0 ± 0.96**, and **44.7 ± 1.5 µm**, or CVs of approximately **4.5%, 4.2%, and 3.4%**. These spreads combine container, subsampling, and analytical effects under one laboratory’s procedure; neither set is a separately estimated within-laboratory repeatability SD or between-laboratory reproducibility SD. NIST describes its dispersion medium as isopropanol and its measurement procedure as 25 measurements after sonication followed by three sets of six measurements checked for consistency. (slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 8-12, slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 3-4)

An actual **between-laboratory** round robin in an NPL good-practice guide used **silica, not metal powder**. For its powder extending to approximately 100 µm, D10/D50/D90 between-laboratory CVs were **30.5%/14.0%/7.4%** with a less prescribed procedure and **9.9%/5.0%/4.6%** after a more closely specified procedure. For finer silica extending to approximately 10 µm, the corresponding CVs were **43.7%/20.4%/8.8%** and **35.2%/9.6%/9.5%**. These results demonstrate the potentially large contribution of laboratory-specific sampling and dispersion; they are **not** ISO 13320 or ASTM B822 precision-and-bias limits for metal powders. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 40-44)

## 3. SEM and dynamic image analysis: circularity or sphericity

**There is no source-supported fixed number of particles that guarantees a stable shape mean.** For a *number-weighted* mean of independently sampled particle circularities, a defensible count is determined from the observed between-particle standard deviation, \(s_C\): its sampling standard error is approximately \(s_C/\sqrt n\), and an approximate 95% sampling half-width is \(1.96s_C/\sqrt n\). For illustration—not a measured AM-powder precision claim—if \(s_C=0.10\), **100, 400, and 1,600** representative particles give approximate half-widths of **0.020, 0.010, and 0.005** circularity units, respectively. Independently prepared aliquots and repeated segmentation are still required to assess *measurement* repeatability; counting more particles cannot remove sampling bias or systematic image-analysis error. The result also depends on whether the reported mean is number- or volume-weighted. Mitterlehner and colleagues explicitly use a **volume-weighted** image-analysis sphericity and show that their silhouette-based sphericity definition differs from another commonly termed circularity: in their notation, SPHT = \(4\pi A/P^2=C^2\). (mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 3-4, mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 4-5)

The stakes of the measurand are illustrated by a NIST SEM study of 17-4 steel powder: it estimated that **59,866 particles** were needed for a **95% probability of no more than 3% relative error in a mass-median *size***, and analyzed **more than 69,000**. That is a distribution-percentile, volume/mass-weighted sizing calculation—**not** a minimum count established for mean circularity. For three repeated dynamic-image-analysis measurements, its average standard uncertainty of *volume fraction per size bin* was **0.02 percentage points wet** and **0.06 percentage points dry**; again, neither number is uncertainty of sphericity. (whiting2019uncertaintyofparticle pages 2-3, whiting2019uncertaintyofparticle pages 3-4)

A metal-powder methods comparison provides a useful warning about **between-method differences**, rather than repeatability: volume-based sphericity for one nearly spherical powder was **0.969 by dynamic imaging**, **0.825 by optical microscopy of polished sections**, and **0.898 by micro-CT**. The authors attribute part of the micro-CT discrepancy to its 1-µm voxel resolution. Consequently, a universal claim of, for example, ±0.01 sphericity across SEM, dynamic imaging, and other geometries would not be justified by these data; no validated typical between-laboratory SD for an AM-powder shape mean was located. (mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 10-11, mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof media d1ad888f)

## 4. SEM–EDS composition: Si and Mg in Al-alloy powder

For **polished, homogeneous specimens measured with standards and matrix corrections**, NIST authors describe achievable relative accuracy of approximately **±5% for major constituents** (>10 wt%), **±10% for minor constituents** (1–10 wt%), and **±25% for trace-level constituents** (0.1–1 wt%). These are accuracy guidance, **not repeatability SDs or validated limits for an unpolished AlSi10Mg particle**. Silicon near 10 wt% lies on the major/minor boundary; magnesium below 1 wt% lies in the authors’ trace category. Surface curvature and local topography of loose particles can cause substantially greater error; normalizing a standardless analysis to 100% can conceal it. (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25)

As an illustration of *best-controlled repeatability*, not of Al-alloy-powder performance, NIST measured a homogeneous reference **glass** in nine replicate standards-based EDS analyses. Si was **25.38 wt% certified versus 25.65 wt% measured** (**+1.1% relative deviation; 0.09% relative replicate SD**), and Mg was **8.85 versus 8.81 wt%** (**−0.4% relative deviation; 0.13% relative replicate SD**). These high Mg and Si concentrations and polished-glass geometry cannot establish precision for approximately 0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in loose AlSi10Mg powder. No Al-alloy-powder-specific interlaboratory SEM–EDS Si/Mg repeatability or reproducibility estimates were verified. Bulk certification of such low Mg contents should therefore be checked with a validated bulk-composition method rather than inferred from particle-surface EDS alone. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 5-6, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25)

## 5. Powder sampling and its share of total variance

A published powder-sampling comparison reproduced in the NPL guide gives **relative SDs/CVs** of **6.81% for coning and quartering, 5.14% for scoop sampling, 2.09% for table splitting, 1.01% for chute splitting, and 0.125% for a spinning riffler**. These characterize that comparison’s sampled property and powder, **not** a universal CV of every sieve cut or D-value and **not** an ASTM B215 precision-and-bias statement. The guide identifies B215 as a practice for sampling metal powders and recommends taking increments across a moving powder stream; it also notes that segregation adds error beyond fundamental random sampling. A separate experiment with segregating glass-particle mixtures found that a rotary divider could introduce composition-dependent bias, underscoring that owning a rotary device does not itself validate unbiased splitting. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 22-26, hawkins1988demonstratingthesampling pages 2-3, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 59-64, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 64-70)

For **independent, approximately unbiased** sources expressed in the *same measurand and units*, a practical variance budget is \(s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\approx s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}}+s^2_{\mathrm{preparation}}+s^2_{\mathrm{instrument}}\). The sampling contribution is \((s^2_{\mathrm{bulk/increment}}+s^2_{\mathrm{split}})/s^2_{\mathrm{total}}\), not the sum of their CVs. The published **0.125%** spinning-riffler CV cannot be inserted directly into an AM-powder D90 or sieve-cut budget: first measure the variation among **independently split test portions**, then compare it with repeated analyses of one portion. As a conditional arithmetic example, if a given measurand has a measured sampling CV of **1%** and analytical CV of **2%**, independent sources imply total CV **2.24%** and sampling accounts for **20% of variance**. Segregation or systematic bias must be assessed separately, not hidden inside this quadrature calculation. (mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 22-26, hawkins1988demonstratingthesampling pages 3-4)

**Bottom line:** the defensible numerical evidence is strongest for NIST’s *single-laboratory, between-container* metal-powder D-value spreads, the *non-metal* laser-diffraction interlaboratory comparison, calibrated-versus-rough-specimen EDS performance, and a *material-specific* splitter comparison. Requested ASTM/ISO **sieve-cut mass-fraction SDs**, metal-powder LD **between-lab CVs**, shape-mean **repeatability SDs**, and AlSi10Mg-specific **Si/Mg EDS repeatability** remain unquantified by the verified sources; assigning them universal numerical tolerances would conflate different measurands and experimental designs. (brown2016interlaboratorystudyfor pages 2-3, slotwinski2014characterizationofmetal pages 8-12, mingard2009improvingtheconsistency pages 40-44, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, mitterlehner2021comparativeevaluationof pages 10-11)

info.query: What is the measurement repeatability (within-lab) and reproducibility (between-lab) of metal powder characterization used for additive manufacturing: (1) sieve analysis per ASTM B214 / ISO 4497 (standard deviation of mass fraction per sieve cut); (2) laser diffraction per ISO 13320 / ASTM B822 (coefficient of variation of D10, D50, D90); (3) SEM or dynamic image analysis of sphericity or circularity (how many particles must be measured for a stable mean, and the typical uncertainty); (4) SEM-EDS quantitative composition of aluminum alloy powders, e.g. Si and Mg in Al alloys (typical relative error and repeatability); (5) powder sampling error (riffling, spinning riffler per ASTM B215) and its contribution to the total variance. Give numeric values with citations, especially ASTM/ISO precision-and-bias statements and interlaboratory studies.
